facts.claim: OPOWER Home Energy Report trials across about 600,000 households reduced average electricity use by 2.0 percent.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because neighbor comparison and tailored tips supplied salient feedback that ordinary bills lacked.
facts.commonError: The reduction came from an 11-to-20-percent electricity price increase.
facts.whyWrong: The reports were a nonprice intervention, though their effect was comparable to such a short-run price change.

facts.claim: The Toxics Release Inventory originated in the 1986 Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because facility-level publication exposed emissions to communities, investors, and peer comparison.
facts.commonError: TRI data remained confidential inside the EPA.
facts.whyWrong: Public access is the mechanism that creates reputational pressure.

facts.claim: A climate club pairs a shared carbon commitment with penalties on nonmembers.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the external consequence makes free riding less attractive than joining the agreement.
facts.commonError: A climate club relies only on voluntary moral appeals.
facts.whyWrong: Its distinctive feature is an enforceable penalty, commonly a trade measure.

facts.claim: The social cost of carbon estimates the damage caused by one additional ton of carbon dioxide emissions.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because monetizing marginal harm provides a benchmark for taxes and regulatory benefit calculations.
facts.commonError: It is the market price firms already pay for every ton emitted.
facts.whyWrong: The social cost is an estimate of external damage, not necessarily an enacted price.

facts.claim: A carbon tax changes incentives by charging for each unit of emissions.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the price makes some external harm part of the emitter's private cost.
facts.commonError: A carbon tax guarantees an exact emissions quantity.
facts.whyWrong: It fixes a price; the resulting quantity depends on behavioral and technological response.

facts.claim: Cap-and-trade fixes an aggregate emissions limit and allows permits to be exchanged.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because trading directs reductions toward sources with lower abatement costs while the cap controls total authorized emissions.
facts.commonError: Permit trading removes the emissions limit.
facts.whyWrong: The number of permits remains bounded by the cap.

facts.claim: Present bias hinders climate action because mitigation costs arrive before many benefits.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because immediate taxes, prices, or restrictions receive more decision weight than avoided harms decades later.
facts.commonError: Delay makes future climate damage economically irrelevant.
facts.whyWrong: Discounting changes present valuation but does not eliminate future welfare.

facts.claim: Conditional cooperators reduce contributions when they believe others are free riding.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because willingness to bear a shared cost depends partly on expectations that peers will reciprocate.
facts.commonError: Public-good contributions are independent of others' behavior.
facts.whyWrong: Observed cooperation often decays when defection becomes visible.

facts.claim: Green More Tomorrow would commit to a modest current carbon cost that rises on a schedule.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because gradual escalation reduces immediate loss salience while locking in stronger future incentives.
facts.commonError: The proposal keeps carbon prices permanently low.
facts.whyWrong: Its defining feature is precommitted increase over time.
